newsitem.title: POLAND: POLISH C.BANK SAYS NOMINAL RATES MIGHT NOT CHANGE OVER LONGER-TERM. [CORRECTED 17:15 GMT]
newsitem.headline: POLISH C.BANK SAYS NOMINAL RATES MIGHT NOT CHANGE OVER LONGER-TERM. [CORRECTED 17:15 GMT]

text.p: (Corrects headline and text to make clear the bank might, not will, keep rates stable).
The National Bank of Poland President Hanna Gronkiewicz-Waltz said on Friday the central bank might keep interest rates unchanged over a long period of time, around six months.
Gronkiewicz-Waltz also said inflation in December 1996 should not exceed 18 percent in year-on-year terms.

"Next year's (government) plan to cut inflation to 13 percent requires a restrictive monetary policy...first of all interest rate policy and this may assume even a lack of a interest rate cut over a long period of time -- I mean a period of six months," she told a news conference.

In a statement issued after the conference the bank said its interest rate policy would be "correlated with its exchange rate policy in such a way that growth in money supply would suport the achievement of the inflation target."
"This means, that the level of nominal interest rates may remain relatively stable over longer periods," the bank statement said.
Gronkiewicz-Waltz also said at the conference a significant expansion in credit action might even call for a small market rate rise in future.
Speaking about inflation prospects for this and next year Gronkiewicz-Waltz said:
"I believe inflation will be no higher than 20 percent this year and I still have a feeling it will not exceed 18 percent."

She said however the government efforts to slash inflation this year from September's 19.5 percent year-on-year, by putting off increases of some officially-controlled prices, could result in higher inflationary pressure next year.
"Some inflationary impulse may carry-over from this year to 1997 because of delayed increases in officially controlled prices," Gronkiewicz-Waltz said.

Earlier this month the central bank said it would try to contain fast growth of credit by boosting real interest rates either through keeping its nominal rates unchanged or ensuring that official rates decline slower than inflation.
But the NBP also reassured markets that it had no plans for a nominal rate rise.
